```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
models <- utils::read.csv("rhc-models.csv")
study <- utils::read.csv("rhc-study.csv")
value <- function(name) study$value[study$quantity == name]
number <- function(x) format(x, big.mark = ",")
three <- function(x) sprintf("%.3f", x)
kept <- models[models$passed_quality_gate, ]
excluded <- models[!models$passed_quality_gate, ]
logistic <- models[models$model_id == "logistic_regression_1", ]
best_logloss <- min(models$logloss)
logloss_limit <- best_logloss * 1.05
percent_above_best <- function(x) sprintf("%.1f %%", 100 * (x / best_logloss - 1))
odds_ratio_min <- sprintf("%.2f", min(kept$odds_ratio))
odds_ratio_max <- sprintf("%.2f", max(kept$odds_ratio))
model_name <- function(id) {
  if (id == "logistic_regression_1") return("logistic regression")
  paste0(toupper(sub("_.*$", "", id)), " seed ", sub("^.*_", "", id))
}
lowest <- kept$model_id[which.min(kept$odds_ratio)]
highest <- kept$model_id[which.max(kept$odds_ratio)]
extreme_names <- if (all(startsWith(c(lowest, highest), "bart_"))) {
  paste0("two BART fits that differ only in their random seed (", model_name(lowest), " and ",
         model_name(highest), ")")
} else {
  paste0(model_name(lowest), " and ", model_name(highest))
}
best_smd <- min(models$smd_max_main)
balance_limit <- min(best_smd + 0.10, 0.25)
odds_ratio <- function(id) sprintf("%.2f", models$odds_ratio[models$model_id == id])
interval <- function(id) {
  row <- models[models$model_id == id, ]
  sprintf("%.2f to %.2f", row$conf_low, row$conf_high)
}
```

This article explains the method behind propsens one idea at a time. Each idea has a short
definition, a concrete example and the numbers of one real study. For the short version, see
[propsens at a glance](at-a-glance.html).

**The example study.** Right heart catheterization measures pressures in the heart and lungs of
critically ill patients. A landmark observational study (Connors et al., *JAMA* 1996) compared
patients who were catheterized within 24 hours of admission with patients who were not. Its
public data have `r number(value("patients"))` patients, `r number(value("treated"))` of them
catheterized (the **treated patients**), with 50 characteristics recorded at admission:
diagnosis, age, coexisting illnesses, vital signs, laboratory values and more. The outcome is
death within 30 days.

## 1. Propensity score and matching

A **propensity score** is one number per patient: the chance, given everything recorded at
admission, that this patient receives the treatment. Two patients with similar scores looked
equally likely to be catheterized on arrival, even if only one of them was.

**Matching** uses the score to build a fair comparison. Each treated patient is paired with an
untreated patient whose score is close, the treated patient's **matched partner**. If the two
matched groups look alike at admission, a difference in their outcomes is less likely to reflect
how ill they were to begin with.

![Matching on the propensity score.](img/works-matching.png){width=100% alt="Patients lined up along an arrow labelled ‘Chance of treatment (propensity score)’. Treated patients wear orange, untreated patients grey. Arcs join each treated patient to the closest untreated patient; the two untreated patients with the lowest scores are left without a partner. Text below: Each treated patient is paired with the closest untreated patient."}

The score is not observed; it has to be estimated with a statistical model, the **propensity
model**. propsens fits several propensity models. Each model is then used to match the patients
with the matching settings chosen for this illustration: 1:1 nearest-neighbour matching without
replacement, with a caliper (a maximum allowed distance between partners) of 0.2 standard
deviations of the logit of the score. Only the propensity model changes; everything else stays
the same.

In the example, each matched design kept between `r sprintf("%.0f %%", 100 * value("treated_kept_min"))`
and `r sprintf("%.0f %%", 100 * value("treated_kept_max"))` of the catheterized patients; the
others had no unused untreated patient within the caliper. With a caliper, the matched estimate
describes the retained treated patients, not all of them.

## 2. The three kinds of model

![The three kinds of propensity model.](img/works-models.png){width=100% alt="Three cards. Logistic regression: a fixed weight for each characteristic. BART: many small decision rules added up. GRF: many decision trees averaged."}

- **Logistic regression** gives each characteristic a fixed weight and adds them up. It is the
  usual choice in published matched studies.
- **BART** (Bayesian additive regression trees) adds up many small decision rules, such as
  "age above 70 and low blood pressure". It picks up combinations of characteristics on its own.
- **GRF** (a generalized random forest) grows many decision trees, each on a random part of the
  data, and averages their answers.

**Seeds.** BART and GRF use randomness while they are fitted, so propsens runs each of them three
times with different random starts (seeds). With logistic regression this gives seven models.
Every score is **cross-fitted**: the patients are split into five groups, and each patient's
score comes from a model fitted on the other four, so no model is judged on patients it has
already seen. The split into groups and the random starts both come from one number, `seed`;
on small data the results can change noticeably with it, so rerun with two or three values
(`seed_sensitivity()` does this) and report all of them.

**Why similarly good models can still disagree.** Think of two experienced clinicians who triage
about as well overall: they agree on most patients, yet they do not rank every patient in the
same place. Propensity models behave the same way. Two models can predict treatment about as well
and still place an individual patient a little higher or lower. In matching, a small change in
position can mean a different partner.

## 3. The quality gate

A model that fits the data poorly will disagree with the others for an uninteresting reason: it
is less accurate. Only disagreement among models a careful researcher would accept tells
us something about the design. So before anything is measured, each of the seven models must
pass two checks, the **quality gate**.

![The quality gate: two checks, fit and balance.](img/works-gate.png){width=100% alt="Two wooden gates on a path. The first is labelled ‘Fits as well as the best’, the second ‘Balances as well as the best’. Three GRF figures stand at the start beside a sign ‘Not kept for this study’; logistic regression and three BART figures stand past both gates under a sign ‘Kept models’."}

**Check 1: fit.** Fit is measured with the **log-loss**, a penalty for each patient that depends
on the chance the model gave to what actually happened. A catheterized patient who was given a
90 % chance of catheterization gets a small penalty (0.11); one who was given a 10 % chance gets
a large penalty (2.30). The log-loss is the average penalty over all patients; lower is better.
It is like the c-statistic, but it also checks whether the predicted chances are right in size,
not only whether they put patients in the right order. A model passes if its log-loss is at most
5 % above the best model's.

In the example, the best log-loss was `r three(best_logloss)` (BART), so the limit was about
`r three(logloss_limit)`. Logistic regression had `r three(logistic$logloss)`
(`r percent_above_best(logistic$logloss)` higher) and passed. The three GRF fits had
`r three(mean(excluded$logloss))` (`r percent_above_best(mean(excluded$logloss))` higher) and
failed.

**Check 2: balance.** The **standardized mean difference (SMD)** of a characteristic is the
difference between the averages of the two matched groups, divided by the spread of that
characteristic; 0.10 or less is commonly accepted as good balance. For each model, propsens takes
the largest SMD over all characteristics after matching. A model passes if this value is at most
0.10 above the best model's, and never above 0.25.

In the example, the best value was `r three(best_smd)`, so the limit was
`r three(balance_limit)`. Logistic regression and the three BART fits reached
`r three(min(kept$smd_max_main))` to `r three(max(kept$smd_max_main))` and passed; the three GRF
fits reached `r three(min(excluded$smd_max_main))` to `r three(max(excluded$smd_max_main))` and
failed.

**Result:** `r value("models_kept")` of `r value("models")` models were kept, logistic regression
and the three BART fits. These are the **kept models** whose disagreement is measured next. Here
two algorithms were kept; when the kept models are seeds of a single algorithm, propsens raises
a warning, because their disagreement then measures only that algorithm's seed noise.

![The quality gate in the heart catheterization example.](rhc-gate.png){width=100% alt="The quality gate in the example. Left panel: cross-fitted log-loss of each of the seven models; right panel: the largest SMD after matching. Dashed lines mark the limits. Logistic regression and BART seeds 1 to 3 lie at or left of both lines and are kept; GRF seeds 1 to 3 lie to the right of both lines and are excluded."}

```{r model-table, echo = FALSE}
algorithm_name <- c(logistic_regression = "Logistic regression", bart = "BART",
                    grf_probability = "GRF")
seed_text <- ifelse(models$algorithm == "logistic_regression", "",
                    paste0(", seed ", sub("^.*_", "", models$model_id)))
model_table <- data.frame(
  Model = paste0(algorithm_name[models$algorithm], seed_text),
  `Log-loss` = three(models$logloss),
  `Largest SMD after matching` = three(models$smd_max_main),
  `Treated patients kept` = sprintf("%.0f %%", 100 * models$treated_kept),
  Kept = ifelse(models$passed_quality_gate, "yes", "no"),
  check.names = FALSE
)
knitr::kable(model_table, align = "lrrrc")
```

**When fewer than two models pass**, there is no set of similarly good models to compare.
propsens then uses all seven models, raises an R warning, and its output opens with it: the
values describe all models, not a kept set. This did not happen in the example.

## 4. All three excluded models are GRF. Is GRF a poor method?

Not in general. The three GRF fits are the same method with different random starts, so they
usually pass or fail together. The gate judges each study on its own data, and in other data GRF
may fit best. In the author's unpublished evaluation runs (matching without replacement), at
least one GRF fit passed the gate in 790 of 800 benchmark datasets based on ACIC 2016 covariates
and in 105 of 300 simulated datasets; in 78 of those 300 the gate kept fewer than two models.

## 5. Rank disagreement and pair instability

A patient's **percentile rank** is their place in the line-up of all patients ordered by the
propensity score, from 0 (lowest chance of treatment) to 100 (highest); the package stores it on
a 0 to 1 scale. Matching pairs patients who stand close together in this line-up, so the order is
what decides who is paired with whom.

![The same patients, lined up slightly differently by each model.](img/works-ranks.png){width=100% alt="Three rows of the same six patients, A to F, one row per model (logistic regression, BART, GRF). Patient C is highlighted: third in the first row, fourth in the BART row and second in the GRF row. Text below: The same patients, lined up slightly differently by each model."}

Each model lines up the same patients. Here patient C moves one place with BART and one place
the other way with GRF. **Rank disagreement** (the primary summary) measures how much such
positions move, on average across the treated patients: for each treated patient it takes the
spread (standard deviation) of their percentile rank across the kept models, and then averages
over the treated patients. 0 would mean every kept model puts every patient in the same place.
Because it is a standard deviation over models, it also depends on how many seeds each kept
algorithm has; propsens also reports a version with equal weight per algorithm (exploratory).

In the example, rank disagreement was **`r three(value("rank_disagreement"))`**: the standard
deviation of a catheterized patient's percentile rank across the four kept models averaged
`r sprintf("%.1f", 100 * value("rank_disagreement"))` points on the 0 to 100 scale. No thresholds
for a "large" value exist yet. The figure shows the real line-ups.

![The catheterized patients' ranks under logistic regression and each kept BART model.](rhc-ranks.png){width=100% alt="The 2,184 catheterized patients, each a dot, ranked by logistic regression (horizontal axis) and by each kept BART model (vertical axis, one panel per seed). On the dashed diagonal both models agree; most dots lie near it, with a visible spread."}

**Pair instability** (exploratory) looks at the partners directly: it measures how often the
kept models choose different untreated partners for the same treated patient. For each treated
patient, propsens finds the partner chosen most often and the share of kept models that chose it;
pair instability is 1 minus the average of that share. With four kept models it lies between 0
(all four always agree) and 0.75 (all four always choose differently).

In the example, pair instability was **`r sprintf("%.2f", value("pair_instability"))`**: on
average, a catheterized patient's most common partner was chosen by only about a third of the
kept models. Of the `r number(value("treated_matched_by_all_kept"))` catheterized patients matched
by all four kept models,
`r if (value("share_with_more_than_one_partner") == 1) "every one" else sprintf("%.0f %%", 100 * value("share_with_more_than_one_partner"))`
had at least two different partners. This is expected when many untreated patients have similar
scores, and it does not by itself mean the matched groups differ; a different partner with the
same characteristics is harmless. Pair instability depends on the number of kept models (its
maximum is 1 minus 1 divided by the number of models) and on how dense the untreated patients
are. The figure follows one typical patient.

![One treated patient, four kept models, four different untreated partners.](rhc-partners.png){width=100% alt="One treated (catheterized) patient on the left, linked to the four kept models: logistic regression and BART seeds 1, 2 and 3. Each model places the patient at a slightly different percentile rank, between about 32 and 43, and pairs the patient with a different untreated patient, A to D."}

propsens also reports the **bootstrap rank instability** of the logistic model (descriptive):
how much the ranks move when the same logistic model is refitted on resampled copies of the
data. It describes the sampling noise of one model rather than the choice between models, and
it is reported alongside rank disagreement. In the example it was
`r three(value("bootstrap_rank_instability"))`.

## 6. Effect estimates across the kept models

propsens never uses the outcome. Only as an illustration, the effect can be estimated with each
kept model's matched pairs; this is not part of the diagnostic. The result is an **odds ratio**: how the
odds of death within 30 days compare between catheterized patients and their untreated
partners. An odds ratio of 1 means no difference; the **95 % confidence interval** is the range of
values compatible with the data.

![Odds ratios of death within 30 days across the four kept models.](rhc-effects.png){width=100% alt="Odds ratio of death within 30 days in the matched pairs of each of the four kept models, with 95 % confidence intervals: logistic regression and BART with seeds 1, 2 and 3. All four lie above 1, between about 1.27 and 1.38; the BART seed 3 estimate is marked as having a largest SMD slightly above 0.10."}

The odds ratio was `r odds_ratio("logistic_regression_1")` (95 % CI
`r interval("logistic_regression_1")`) with logistic regression, and `r odds_ratio("bart_1")`
(`r interval("bart_1")`), `r odds_ratio("bart_2")` (`r interval("bart_2")`) and
`r odds_ratio("bart_3")` (`r interval("bart_3")`) with the three BART models. All four
estimates lie above 1 (higher odds of death among catheterized patients than among their matched
untreated partners).

Matching with each kept model gave odds ratios between `r odds_ratio_min` and
`r odds_ratio_max`, all with wide and overlapping 95 % confidence intervals. The two ends of this
range are `r extreme_names`, and each matched sample keeps a different
`r sprintf("%.0f", 100 * value("treated_kept_min"))` to
`r sprintf("%.0f", 100 * value("treated_kept_max"))` % of the catheterized patients, so the
estimates describe slightly different groups. The example shows that the estimate is not
identical across kept models; it does not show how much of the difference is due to the model,
to the seed, or to chance. A larger disagreement does not by itself mean a larger change in the
estimate.

The third BART model's largest SMD after matching
(`r three(models$smd_max_main[models$model_id == "bart_3"])`) is above the conventional 0.10
although it passes the relative rule of the gate; an analyst using the fixed 0.10 rule
(`balance_rule = "absolute"`) would not keep it.

## How the numbers were produced

The seven models take about 16 minutes on one core, so this article shows the code without
running it. The full script, which also draws the figures, is
`data-raw/heart_catheterization_example.R` in the package's source repository. The
characteristics and the treatment come from `ATbounds::RHC`; the outcome, death within 30 days,
is read from the public raw file of the Vanderbilt Department of Biostatistics
(<https://hbiostat.org/data/repo/rhc.csv>) after its checksum is checked. No patient-level data
are stored in propsens.

```{r reproduce, eval = FALSE}
library(propsens)
# `cohort`: ATbounds::RHC with its dummy columns turned back into the 50 admission
# characteristics (see data-raw/heart_catheterization_example.R); `swang1` = catheterized.
formula <- reformulate(setdiff(names(cohort), "swang1"), response = "swang1")
result <- propensity_sensitivity(formula, data = cohort, replace = FALSE, caliper = 0.2,
                                 cores = 1, seed = 1)
result           # the gate, rank disagreement, pair instability
summary(result)  # every model's fit and balance
```

The odds ratios are conditional odds ratios for 1:1 matched pairs: the number of pairs in which
only the catheterized patient died, divided by the number in which only the untreated partner
died, with a Wald interval on the log scale. The exact definitions of every diagnostic are in
`vignette("definitions", package = "propsens")`.
